schools.summary: Gill reads 'God of my righteousness' as the righteous God who vindicates David's innocence and authors and imputes his righteousness through his Son; Calvin, 'the maintainer of my right,' has David appeal from men's slander to God, referring the psalm to Saul's persecution and reading 'enlarged' as room made when he was besieged.

Keil and Delitzsch call it the Davidic evening hymn paired with Psalm 3 and open the study of the heading 'to the chief Musician'; Ellicott renders 'In my crying hear me,' hails God as the eternal source of righteousness ('shall not the judge of all the earth do right?'), and glosses 'enlarged' as 'in my straitness thou hast made room for me' (cf. Ps. 18:19).

Henry expounds the title — the chief Musician and the Neginoth or stringed instruments (Hab. 3:19), the melody now made in the heart — and pleads 'God of my righteousness' as author of David's righteous disposition and patron of his cause, resting all on 'hear me for thy mercy's sake'; Spurgeon notes the title is unique in Scripture and makes God the author, witness, maintainer, judge, and rewarder of David's righteousness.

Clarke derives Neginoth from a root 'to strike,' reads an evening hymn before rest, and takes 'thou hast enlarged me' of one brought from prison into the open; Wesley glosses God as 'the witness and defender of my righteous cause.'

Augustine reads the psalm christologically — the words of the risen Lord, or of the believer in the Church hoping on him — taking 'in tribulation thou hast enlarged me' as the soul led from the straits of sadness into the broad ways of joy.

debates.question: What is the occasion of the psalm?

sides.position: Saul's persecution, the long struggle implied by the 'how long' of v.2
Absalom's rebellion, the evening companion to the morning hymn of Psalm 3

outliers.note: Reads the whole psalm allegorically as the words of Christ after the Resurrection, or of the believing soul in the Church, rather than as David's historical prayer.

themes: to the chief Musician on Neginoth
thou hast enlarged me in distress
hear me for thy mercy's sake

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch distinguish 'sons of ish' (the prominent) from 'sons of Adam' (the multitude), aiming the address at the aristocratic party behind Absalom; Ellicott reads 'men of high degree' (Luther's 'gentlemen'), infers the calumny had reached the king, and records the LXX/Vulg. variant 'how long will ye be heavy of heart?'
Gill takes the 'sons of men' for the nobles drawn into the conspiracy, and 'vanity' and 'leasing' for the wickedness and the lies they loved and pursued against David.

Henry hears a double charge — the sinners debase themselves as 'sons of men' (man the noble creature) and dishonour their Maker, turning his glory into shame as the idolaters of Rom. 1:23; 'glory' may mean God himself, whom David called his glory (Ps. 3:3); Spurgeon admires David's undaunted courage, chiding his great enemies as foolish children who make his honour a jest, and pausing at the 'Selah.'

Clarke reads 'leasing' as lying and the whole as Absalom's empty promises, marking the 'Selah' — 'see what the end will be'; Wesley refers 'my glory' to the honour God had conferred on David, and 'vanity/lying' to his enemies' calumnies.

outliers.note: Notes that the Septuagint and Vulgate followed a different and perhaps correct reading of the clause, 'how long will ye be heavy (slow) of heart?'

schools.summary: Clarke reads 'set apart' as God marking the pious, tender-hearted man for his own property, not to be touched; Wesley makes the godly man David himself, pronounced a man after God's own heart (1 Sam. 13:14) and set apart to be God's vicegerent.

Ellicott traces the verb to the severance of Israel from Egypt (Exod. 8:22), 'to distinguish or honour,' and stresses that chasid names the covenant relation more than moral excellence; Keil and Delitzsch read a summons to the adversaries to repent and cleave to the Lord.

Henry presses it two ways — a warning that to touch God's set-apart ones is to touch the apple of his eye (Matt. 18:6; Exod. 22:23), and an assurance that every godly man is God's sealed jewel; Spurgeon turns it to the comfort of election, the guarantee of complete salvation and an argument for success at the throne of grace ('shall not God avenge his own elect?').
Gill fixes on the confidence that follows — 'the LORD will hear when I call unto him' — bidding the reader depend on it as fact.

themes: the LORD hath set apart the godly
the LORD will hear when I call

schools.summary: Gill glosses 'stand in awe' as fear of God and his judgments, but records the LXX/Vulg./Syriac/Arabic/Ethiopic 'be ye angry, and sin not' (taken up in Eph. 4:26) and weighs sinful against righteous anger.

Keil and Delitzsch judge the Septuagint 'be angry, and sin not' the correct rendering, a warning against blind passion; Ellicott calls 'be angry,' though etymologically correct and rightly quoted at Ephesians, 'plainly inadmissible here,' and renders 'tremble.'

Clarke leans to 'if ye be angry... let not your disaffection carry you to rebellion,' and renders 'be still' as 'be dumb'; Wesley keeps the reverential 'be afraid... of God, who hath engaged in my cause.'

Henry, noting the LXX's 'be angry' in passing, expounds 'stand in awe' as a holy reverence of God's majesty and dread of his wrath, and 'commune with your heart upon your bed' as night self-examination (Ps. 63:6); Spurgeon presses 'tremble and sin not — how many reverse this counsel and sin but tremble not.'

debates.question: Does the Hebrew of the verse mean 'stand in awe / tremble' or 'be ye angry' (the LXX rendering quoted at Ephesians 4:26)?

sides.position: 'stand in awe / tremble' — reverent fear of God (the received sense)
'be ye angry, and sin not' — a caution against sinful anger, the LXX reading Paul adopts

themes: stand in awe, and sin not
be ye angry, and sin not (LXX, Eph. 4:26)
commune with your heart upon your bed

schools.summary: Gill ranges the senses of 'sacrifices of righteousness' — righteously-gotten offerings, lawful and unblemished, above all offered in the faith of the great sacrifice, and even alms and beneficence God prefers to ceremony.

Ellicott takes them narrowly as 'right' or 'due' sacrifices, duly performed (cf. Deut. 33:19); Keil and Delitzsch bind the offering to the trust that follows as the counsel turning the disaffected back to the Lord.

Clarke warns that no sacrifice offered in rebellion is received, and that under the gospel none is accepted but through Christ's one atoning sacrifice; Wesley requires the offerer be righteous and offer with faith and true repentance.

Henry joins the halves — sacrifices of righteousness are good works, better than burnt-offerings, while the unrighteous man's offering is an abomination (Isa. 1:11) — then 'put your trust in the LORD'; Spurgeon hears the whole gospel in it, the righteous sacrifice setting forth the sin-atoning Lamb, and points sinners to trust in him who is the Lord Jehovah.

themes: no sacrifice without a right heart
put your trust in the LORD

schools.summary: Ellicott hears the despairing cry from within David's camp, keeps the future 'who will shew us,' and finds in 'lift up the light of thy countenance' an echo of the priestly benediction (Num. 6:24) with a play on the word for a banner; Keil and Delitzsch read it as the voice of companions whose long tribulation has turned hope to despair.

Wesley takes the 'many' for David's own followers weary of waiting on God; Clarke objects that 'any' is not in the text ('Who will shew us good?'), the universal search of man for a good he mistakes for sensual gratification, and names the light of God's countenance the supreme good.

Henry makes the 'many' carnal worldlings whose foolish wish seeks a good that can be seen and any good rather than the chief good, against which the godly pray for the light of God's face — the eye of faith looking beyond the eye of sense (2 Cor. 4:18); Spurgeon owns the craving to see rather than believe as 'the tendency of us all,' the believer's face turned upward like the angels'.
Gill allows several readings of the 'many' — David's men longing for home, or enemies wishing Absalom's success — but sets first the carnal, worldly-minded seeking temporal good.

debates.question: Who are the 'many that say, Who will shew us any good?'

sides.position: carnal worldlings, or mankind at large, seeking a merely sensible good

outliers.note: Objects that the Authorized Version's 'any' is not in the Hebrew — the text reads simply 'Who will shew us good?'

themes: who will shew us any good
lift up the light of thy countenance
the chief good against sensible good

schools.summary: Henry weighs the gladness God put in David's heart against the worldlings' corn and wine: when God gives grace he gives gladness, an inward, substantial joy surpassing the joy of harvest, while the worldling's mirth is a flash whose laughter hides a sorrowful heart (Prov. 14:13); true joy is God's gift, not as the world gives (John 14:27), so the saints may pity, not envy, the prosperous.

themes: thou hast put gladness in my heart
the mirth of the world a flash

schools.summary: Henry unfolds 'I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep': assured of God's favour David rests as gladly as those whose harvest is full (Boaz, Ruth 3:7), for the LORD only makes him dwell in safety — alone yet not alone; he gathers it into three assurances (rest in God, security from enemies even in the sleep of death with Simeon, Luke 2:29, and committing all to God like the sleeping husbandman, Mark 4:26), so the evening prayer ends in mercy and safety.

themes: I will lay me down in peace and sleep
thou only makest me dwell in safety
the sleep of death and Simeon's peace
